n: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, hears reports about Jesus’s growing fame.

f.g: Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome. Tetrarch = ruler of a fourth part of a kingdom.

n: His guilty conscience leads him to a fearful conclusion: Jesus must be John the Baptist come back from the dead.

f.w: he is risen from the dead

n: Matthew flashes back to explain. Herod had imprisoned John because of Herodias, who had left her husband, Herod’s half-brother, to marry Herod.

f.g: A granddaughter of Herod the Great; she married two of her uncles in turn.

n: John had boldly told Herod that this marriage broke God’s law. Prophets speak truth even to powerful rulers.

f.w: It is not lawful for thee to have her

n: Herod wanted John dead but feared a public backlash, since the people regarded John as a prophet.

f.w: they counted him as a prophet

n: At Herod’s birthday banquet, Herodias’s daughter danced for the guests and delighted Herod.

f.g: The historian Josephus names her Salome; she was probably a young teenager.

n: In a rash moment, Herod swore an oath to give her anything she asked.

f.g: Mark adds that he offered up to half his kingdom.

n: Prompted by her vengeful mother, she asks for John’s head on a platter — right then and there.

f.g: charger = a large serving platter.

f.w: being before instructed of her mother
f.g: Having been coached by her mother beforehand.

n: Herod is upset, but pride and fear of losing face before his guests win out over conscience. He grants the request.
John is beheaded in the prison — a martyr for speaking the truth.

f.g: Latter-day Saints believe the resurrected John restored the Aaronic Priesthood in 1829.

n: The horrifying “gift” is carried to the girl, who brings it to her mother.

f.g: damsel = a young girl.

n: John’s loyal disciples bury his body and then go tell Jesus, his cousin and the one John had prepared the way for.
Grieving the news, Jesus seeks solitude by boat. But crowds see where he’s going and hurry around the shore on foot.

f.g: A deserted, uninhabited area — not necessarily sandy desert. Luke places it near Bethsaida.

n: Though he wanted time alone, Jesus is moved with compassion when he sees the crowd and heals their sick.
As evening falls the disciples suggest sending everyone away to buy food in nearby villages.

f.g: victuals (pronounced “vittles”) = food.

n: Jesus surprises them: “You give them something to eat.” He invites them to be part of the solution.
All they have is five loaves and two fish — John’s Gospel says from a boy’s lunch.

f.g: Small flat barley loaves and probably dried or salted fish.

n: Jesus simply says, “Bring them to me.” What we offer him, however small, he can multiply.

f.g: hither = here.

n: Jesus has the people sit, gives thanks, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples to distribute — actions that foreshadow the Last Supper.
Everyone eats until full, and twelve baskets of leftovers remain — more than they started with.

f.g: Possibly one for each apostle; twelve also recalls the tribes of Israel.

n: About 5,000 men were fed, plus women and children — perhaps well over ten thousand people. This is the only miracle besides the Resurrection recorded in all four Gospels.
Jesus immediately sends the disciples off by boat while he dismisses the crowd. John notes the people wanted to make him king by force.

f.g: constrained = urged strongly, made them.

n: Then Jesus climbs a mountain alone to pray, as he often did after demanding days.
Meanwhile the disciples’ boat is far from land, battered by waves and a strong headwind.

f.g: The wind was blowing against them.

n: Between 3 and 6 a.m., after hours of rowing, Jesus comes to them walking on the water.

f.w: the fourth watch of the night
f.g: Romans divided the night into four watches; the fourth ran roughly from 3 to 6 a.m.

n: Terrified, the disciples think they are seeing a ghost and scream in fear.

f.g: A ghost or apparition.

n: Jesus calms them at once: “Take courage; it is I; don’t be afraid.” The words “it is I” echo God’s name, “I AM.”

f.g: Greek egō eimi — literally “I am.”

n: Peter, bold as ever, asks Jesus to call him out onto the water.

f.g: bid = command, invite.

n: At Jesus’s word, Peter steps out of the boat and actually walks on water toward him.
When Peter shifts his focus from Jesus to the wind, fear takes over and he begins to sink. His three-word prayer is enough.

f.g: boisterous = strong, violent.

n: Jesus instantly reaches out and catches him. His gentle rebuke asks Peter to consider why he doubted.
As soon as they climb into the boat, the wind stops.
The disciples worship Jesus and declare that he truly is the Son of God — a major step in their understanding.

f.w: Of a truth thou art the Son of God

n: They land at Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.

f.g: A small fertile plain south of Capernaum; the lake itself was sometimes called the Lake of Gennesaret.

n: Local people recognize Jesus and quickly spread word, bringing all their sick to him.

f.g: Recognized him.

n: Like the woman in chapter 9, they ask only to touch the edge of his cloak — and all who do are healed.

f.g: Completely healed.
